title: The Anthropic Feedback Loop: The Cost of Capital Delusion and Diversion!
gist: Damodaran stress-tests his $1.45T Anthropic valuation, ranking target revenue ($1T in ten years) as the most fragile input and governance, margins, compute needs and regulation next, then argues at length that a 9.74% cost of capital is defensible versus history, market-implied returns and P/E arithmetic, and that VC/PE target returns are fiction.

insights.claim: Damodaran's Anthropic IPO equity value is $1.45 trillion, slightly below his prior $1.475 trillion after updating trailing revenue with leaked Q3 2026 numbers, with next-twelve-month revenue still assumed around $100 billion.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Anchor for IPO pricing debates; his value sits near the low end of offering estimates.

insights.claim: The single most critical and fragile input is target revenue of about $1 trillion in ten years; if it fails, lower growth would push down margins, create idle compute and raise failure risk, so errors in other inputs would compound in the same direction.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Revenue trajectory, not discount rate, is what to debate and monitor.
insights.quote: it is my estimate of the target revenues for Anthropic

insights.claim: Founder-controlled governance (public benefit corporation plus voting-share structure) is a red flag because setbacks require outsiders who can push management to change course.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Governance discount risk for the IPO.

insights.claim: He assumes a 32.5% target operating margin before the regulatory haircut and argues AI will not fully commoditize because stickiness, such as Claude agents combined with client data, can preserve pricing power.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Moat thesis rests on workflow/data lock-in rather than model quality alone.

insights.claim: Data-center build-out is getting harder as local communities push back and politicians find opposing it a net vote winner, threatening the smooth compute expansion in his story.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Local opposition is a physical constraint on AI revenue growth.

insights.claim: He values Anthropic's contractual compute commitments at just over $450B (PV about $373B), against outside estimates of $400-800B, with only about $70B due next year and $76B the year after versus a $114B cash balance expected to exceed $200B post-IPO.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Near-term default risk is low; disclosure of commitment timing remains a gap.
insights.locator: The IPO Valuation / The Cost of Debt

insights.claim: He builds in a 10% failure risk separately from the cost of capital, estimating a BB+ rating, and says a reader worried about default should move failure risk, not the discount rate; jamming it into cost of capital would require roughly 11%.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Separate going-concern discount rate from failure probability.

insights.claim: Regulatory risk worries him most as a place he could be wrong, since one election could bring onerous AI rules that cut revenue and profits rather than a small slice of operating profit.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Political event risk for AI valuations.

insights.claim: Crowd inputs in his shared sheet put the average Anthropic value nearer $1 trillion than $1.5 trillion, with more respondents saying he overvalued, and the top stated reason (excluding 'worth nothing') was a cost of capital that is too low.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Sentiment check: consensus skeptical of his number.

themes.theme: Cost of capital is bounded by reality

insights.claim: The average US equity return was 8.74% (2001-25), 11.92% (1976-2025) and 10.13% (1928-2025), and the premium over 10-year Treasuries was 5.5-5.75%, implying about 10.4-10.65% cost of equity at a 4.9% T-bond on October 26, 2026.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Historical ceiling for cost of equity assumptions.

insights.claim: The market-implied expected return on US equities at the start of October 2026 was 8.99%, model-agnostic, and has not exceeded 10% since 1994.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Claiming 12-15% for a typical firm is not possible in this market.

insights.claim: A 15% cost of equity with ~5% nominal growth and ~20% ROE implies a P/E of about 7.5 versus an actual forward P/E near 20, so insisting on a 15% cost of equity is inconsistent with accepting current valuations.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Use multiples as a consistency test for discount rates.

insights.claim: In technology, 80% of firms have costs of equity between 9.88% and 14.49% and costs of capital between 9.02% and 12.27%, so the range of reasonable discount rates is narrow.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Don't over-engineer the discount rate; it won't move value much.
insights.locator: Cost of Capital - The Cross Section

insights.claim: Cost of capital should rise by differential inflation plus country risk premium for other currencies: about +4.26% for India (median Indian company ~12.05% in rupees) and a median Swiss company around 5.85%.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Currency and country adjustments for non-US valuations.
insights.locator: Cost of Capital - The Cross Section

insights.claim: Pushing Anthropic to a 90th-percentile tech cost of capital of 12% requires setting failure risk to 0% and changing the rate over time as the company scales.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Avoid double-counting failure risk.
insights.locator: Cost of Capital - The Cross Section

insights.claim: VC and PE target returns of 20-50% are fiction: Cambridge Associates data show actual VC and PE returns lag public equity indices over long periods and are far below stated targets.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Discount manager return pitches; compare with index returns.

insights.claim: Promising excessive target returns pushes active investors to chase ten- or hundred-baggers and overreach on risk, and the inflated targets feed back into how much founders must give up for capital.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Return promises distort behavior and terms.

insights.claim: Corporate hurdle rates are often set 2-3% above market-justified levels; this leads managers to inflate cash-flow forecasts, which pushes hurdle rates higher in turn, until both become fictional.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Overstated hurdle rates cause underinvestment as companies mature.

insights.claim: In 2025 fewer than 30% of public companies earned returns on equity or capital above their costs, and fewer than 20% beat their hurdle rates by more than 5%, even using his low cost of capital.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Most companies don't earn their cost of capital.

insights.claim: At a 20% cost of equity no S&P 500 company would appear undervalued, and unrealistically high hurdle rates push individuals toward scams and private-company owners toward selling too cheaply via build-up cost-of-capital methods with thinly sourced premiums.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Beware unrealistic required returns.
insights.locator: Individual Investors and Privately owned businesses

insights.claim: Investors can respond to uncertainty by ignoring it, avoiding it, demanding a margin of safety (which trades off type 1 and type 2 errors) or using diversification and the law of large numbers to hold riskier stocks in small positions.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Position sizing, not paralysis, is his answer to valuation uncertainty; he would not put a $1M portfolio entirely in Anthropic.
